marble.name: Conductors and insulators
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Recognise some common conductors and insulators, and associate metals with being good conductors of electricity
marble.prompt: Can you test objects in a circuit and explain why metal objects let electricity through but rubber and plastic don't?

cluster.summary: Your child is beginning to understand energy — observing how sunlight warms objects and surfaces, and designing simple structures to create shade and reduce warming effects.

misconceptions: 'All metals are magnetic / all shiny things conduct' — conflating conduction with magnetism or shininess; the test, not appearance, decides (a shiny painted surface may not conduct).
Thinking the plastic-coated wire conducts along its plastic, or not realising the metal inside is the conductor and the plastic the insulator.
Believing an insulator in the gap 'slows' the electricity rather than stopping the loop entirely — at this level it simply doesn't light.
Overgeneralising from one metal or assuming non-metals never conduct (graphite/pencil lead is a useful counter-case).
Thinking thickness or size of the object determines conduction rather than the material it is made of.
representations: A gap-in-the-loop test rig with two crocodile clips and a bulb — the canonical conductor/insulator tester.
A predict-test-record results table: material | prediction | conductor or insulator.
A two-column sort: conductors (metals highlighted) vs insulators (wood, plastic, rubber, glass).
A cutaway of an electrical wire: metal core (conductor) inside a plastic sheath (insulator).
authoredAnswer: What decides it is what the material is made of, not how it looks: metals conduct electricity (let current flow through), while most non-metals such as plastic, wood and rubber are insulators (block it). Shininess doesn't decide it — a shiny plastic still blocks current and a dull metal still conducts. The iron conducts because it's a metal; the ruler blocks it because it's plastic.
probe: Offer a shiny plastic object (or foil-covered card) and a dull or rusty metal object. Ask the child to predict which will light the bulb AND why, before testing each in the circuit. The reason exposes the 'shiny conducts' rule; the dull metal lighting up while the shiny plastic fails violates it. Then test both.

wrongAnswers.wrong: The shiny material conducts and the dull one doesn't, because shiny things carry electricity.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Predicts a shiny non-metal (foil-wrapped plastic, shiny painted object) conducts and a dull metal doesn't.
wrongAnswers.fix: Test a dull, unpolished metal against a shiny plastic — the outcome flips the surface rule; sort by 'is it actually a metal?'.

wrongAnswers.wrong: The plastic coating is what carries the electricity along the wire.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Says the coloured plastic sheath conducts.
wrongAnswers.fix: Strip a wire — the metal inside conducts; the plastic is there to insulate and protect so we aren't shocked.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Classifies hard wood or glass as conductors.
wrongAnswers.fix: Test hard glass and hard wood (insulators) against softer metals — hardness isn't the rule, being a metal is.

before.name: Building a simple circuit
before.reason: Must know circuit components before testing which materials conduct electricity
